lessonContentPlans.lessonSummary: Build from charging-system relationships to evidence-based diagnostic decisions using symptoms, measurements, and vehicle-specific verification procedures.

learningObjectives.statement: Explain the functional relationship among the battery, alternator, diode rectifier, voltage regulator, and vehicle electrical loads.
Interpret charging-system symptoms and measurements as evidence rather than as proof of a component failure.
Select and justify a vehicle-specific next diagnostic check using the available evidence.

contentBlocks.title: Lesson targets
contentBlocks.description: Preview the system-understanding, evidence-interpretation, and diagnostic-reasoning outcomes.
teachingPoints: Explain the charging-system relationships used in this lesson model.
Separate symptoms, observations, measurements, hypotheses, and conclusions.
Use a source reference only when its applicability matches the system, voltage domain, test method, and measurement context.
Select a next diagnostic check without treating one symptom or one measurement as proof of component failure.
contentBlocks.learnerAction: Identify which learning objective requires evidence interpretation rather than recall.

contentBlocks.title: Prerequisite check
contentBlocks.description: Activate prior knowledge of circuit behavior, meter use, polarity, and electrical safety.
teachingPoints: Identify source, load, conductor, ground, and test-point roles in a basic electrical circuit.
Review meter polarity and the difference between system-voltage and voltage-drop measurements.
A measured number has meaning only when the operating condition, test location, voltage domain, and units are known.
contentBlocks.learnerAction: Label each sample statement as circuit knowledge, measurement context, or diagnostic conclusion.

contentBlocks.title: Charging-system relationships
contentBlocks.description: Explain how generation, rectification, regulation, storage, and loads interact as one system.
teachingPoints: The cited Frontiers article identifies the alternator as the primary source of electric energy within a vehicle.
The same source describes an automotive alternator as a synchronous AC generator using diode rectification and identifies rotor, stator, diode rectifier, and voltage regulator as core elements.

Delco Remy describes the charging system as an alternator-battery-cable system: the alternator replenishes the battery and provides power for vehicle loads through the charging path, while the battery remains part of the same operating system.
Vehicle-specific topology, charging control strategy, and operating limits must still be verified from applicable service information.
contentBlocks.learnerAction: Trace the simplified energy path from alternator generation through rectification to the vehicle electrical system, then identify where vehicle-specific evidence is required.

evidenceReferences.locator: Tech Tip: Relationship Between Alternator and Batteries; corroborated by Delco Remy Voltage Drop Test, March 14, 2024
evidenceReferences.approval: citation-only external reference; no reusable vendor excerpt stored

contentBlocks.sourceBoundary: Do not convert this general model into a universal wiring diagram, voltage target, charging strategy, or component test procedure.

contentBlocks.title: Symptoms are evidence
contentBlocks.description: Distinguish warning indicators, low-voltage symptoms, and measurements from final diagnostic conclusions.
teachingPoints: A symptom is evidence that a condition exists; it is not proof of which component caused it.
A measurement is evidence only when the test point, operating state, voltage domain, units, and applicable reference are known.
A source-backed value may be a design basis, maximum, minimum, or reference-only value; those roles are not interchangeable.
A diagnostic conclusion should follow from compatible evidence and a verification step.
contentBlocks.learnerAction: Sort sample cards into symptom, measurement, source reference, hypothesis, or conclusion.
contentBlocks.sourceBoundary: This block teaches evidence reasoning and does not assign universal charging-system symptoms to a specific failed component.

contentBlocks.title: Worked diagnostic example
contentBlocks.description: Trace a concern through evidence collection, interpretation, and selection of a next check.
teachingPoints: Start with source applicability before comparing a number: the cited Delco values come from a 12 V charging-cable sizing table, not from a universal diagnostic voltage-drop test procedure.
The source-backed 0.300 V value is the design basis used for the cited new-vehicle cable-sizing table; it is not a universal pass/fail threshold.
The source-backed 0.500 V value is the maximum voltage-drop basis stated for vehicle life within that same cited 12 V cable-sizing context.

A project-authored 0.350 V hypothetical voltage-drop observation is above the 0.300 V design basis but below the 0.500 V maximum. That comparison describes its position relative to the two cited source values; it does not identify a failed component.

Before turning that comparison into a diagnostic decision, verify that the cable path, voltage domain, operating/load condition, test points, and vehicle-specific procedure make the observation legitimately comparable.
contentBlocks.learnerAction: Explain why 0.350 V is above the cited design basis but below the cited maximum, identify what context must be verified before treating it as comparable evidence, and state what additional evidence is needed before naming a failed component.

evidenceReferences.locator: Delco Remy charging-cable requirements, PDF p. 1
Delco Remy charging-cable requirements, PDF p. 1

contentBlocks.sourceBoundary: The 0.350 V value is a project-authored hypothetical training observation, not a vehicle specification or prescribed test result. The Delco 0.300 V and 0.500 V values come from a 12 V charging-cable sizing table and must not be presented as a universal diagnostic procedure.

interpretation: 0.300 V -> cited new-vehicle cable-sizing design basis
0.500 V -> cited vehicle-life maximum voltage-drop basis
0.350 V -> above the design basis and below the cited maximum
No component failure or diagnostic test outcome is established from this comparison alone
requiredContextBeforeDiagnosticUse: cable path or conductor under evaluation

contentBlocks.title: Guided evidence sorting
contentBlocks.description: Classify observations as symptoms, measurements, hypotheses, or verification evidence.
teachingPoints: Case A: 0.180 V is observed, but conductor identity and wiring configuration are unknown. Do not apply the cited 0.200 V 3-wire #2-lead maximum until the source applicability is verified.

Case B: a project-authored 0.550 V hypothetical observation is considered within the cited 12 V charging-cable sizing-table context. Because it is above the cited 0.500 V maximum for that source-scoped charging-cable context, it is outside that source-scoped reference; this alone does not identify which conductor, connection, or component is responsible.

Case C: a charging concern is reported and no measurement has been collected. Identify the operating context, test target, and applicable procedure before gathering discriminating evidence or naming a cause.
contentBlocks.learnerAction: For each case choose comparable, not comparable, or more evidence required. Justify the choice using source applicability, identify any missing measurement context, and avoid converting a reference comparison directly into a component diagnosis.
contentBlocks.sourceBoundary: The 0.200 V and 0.500 V values retain their cited source scope. They do not establish a universal charging-system test procedure, and an out-of-reference value does not by itself identify a failed component.

contentBlocks.title: Independent charging concern
contentBlocks.description: Build and defend a diagnostic plan for a charging-system complaint without being given the answer path.
teachingPoints: The learner receives a charging-system concern and a lesson-safe evidence packet with no preselected failed component or keyed interpretation.
The learner separates known observations from unknown information and identifies which evidence is still required.
The learner forms at least two plausible hypotheses and chooses a next check that can reduce uncertainty between them.
The learner states what result would support or weaken each working hypothesis and stops short of a final component diagnosis until the evidence supports it.
contentBlocks.learnerAction: Choose either the charging-system or electrical-load evidence packet. Write a diagnostic plan containing the concern, known evidence, important unknowns, two plausible hypotheses, the next discriminating check, required source/applicability information, predicted evidence outcomes, and a verification step.
contentBlocks.sourceBoundary: Scenario measurements are project-authored training evidence, not vehicle specifications. No pass/fail meaning or failed component is supplied. Apply an authoritative reference only when its voltage domain, test points, operating/load condition, wiring context, and procedure match.

operatingContext: Vehicle-specific diagnostic procedure and limits intentionally not supplied

observations.meaning: project-authored comparison value; source applicability must be established before interpretation

unknownsToResolve: battery condition and state of charge
vehicle-specific charging strategy and expected behavior
charging-path wiring configuration and conductor identity

independentCases.title: Electrical load with dim and flickering lamps
independentCases.concern: Exterior lamps dim and flicker as accessory electrical load increases.
operatingContext: Accessory load increased for the training case
Vehicle-specific diagnostic procedure and limits intentionally not supplied

observations.meaning: project-authored observation; no pass/fail status assigned

unknownsToResolve: load current and operating condition required by an applicable procedure
vehicle-specific charging strategy and expected behavior
condition of power and ground connections
applicable source limits for the exact test path
independentCases.studentPrompt: Use the raw measurements to decide what remains uncertain. Form two plausible hypotheses and choose a measurement or inspection that would discriminate between them.

contentBlocks.title: Reasoning check
contentBlocks.description: Check system relationships, evidence interpretation, and next-step justification.
teachingPoints: Check 1: explain the functional relationship among the battery, alternator, diode rectifier, voltage regulator, and vehicle electrical loads using the lesson system model and identify which parts require vehicle-specific verification.
Check 2: explain why a design-basis value is not automatically a failure threshold.
Check 3: decide whether a 3-wire #2-lead limit can be used when conductor identity is unknown.
Check 4: distinguish a symptom, measurement, hypothesis, and verified conclusion.
contentBlocks.learnerAction: Answer each check in one or two sentences and name the evidence role used.

contentBlocks.title: Explain and retry
contentBlocks.description: Provide reasoning-focused feedback and allow the learner to revise the diagnostic decision.
teachingPoints: If a learner names a failed component from a symptom alone, return to the evidence-versus-conclusion distinction.
If a learner treats 0.300 V as a universal maximum, point out that the source marks it as a design basis.
If a learner applies the 0.200 V limit without confirming 3-wire/#2-lead applicability, require a context correction before retry.
If a learner treats a project-authored measurement as a source specification, require the evidence roles to be separated.
contentBlocks.learnerAction: Revise one incorrect diagnostic statement so it names the evidence, its limitation, and the next verification step.

contentBlocks.title: Evidence and source boundary
contentBlocks.description: Identify which claims are general principles and which checks require vehicle-specific authoritative information.
teachingPoints: Frontiers source: rights-cleared textual reuse under CC BY 4.0 for the exact hashed article; technical review and chunk approval remain pending.
Delco charging references: use only with their stored system-voltage, test-method, wiring, conductor, and comparison-role applicability.
Delco battery-relationship reference: citation-only external technical reference; no reusable vendor excerpt, figure, or chunk is stored.
Project-authored training measurements: useful for reasoning practice but never promoted to authoritative vehicle specifications.
Vehicle-specific service procedures and limits require an appropriate authoritative source before use on a real vehicle.
contentBlocks.learnerAction: For every technical statement in the worked example and system model, identify whether it comes from a scholarly source, authoritative specification, citation-only external technical reference, project-authored training example, or vehicle-specific service information.

evidenceReferences.approval: citation-only external reference; no reusable vendor excerpt stored

contentBlocks.title: Diagnostic decision summary
contentBlocks.description: Summarize the progression from system understanding to evidence-supported verification.
teachingPoints: Understand the system relationship before interpreting a measurement.
Treat symptoms and measurements as evidence, not automatic diagnoses.
Match every numeric comparison to an applicable source and comparison role.
Keep project-authored training values separate from authoritative specifications.
Choose the next check to reduce uncertainty, then verify the final conclusion using the applicable vehicle-specific procedure and authoritative information.
contentBlocks.learnerAction: Write a five-sentence diagnostic summary moving from concern to evidence, source comparison, next check, and verification without naming a failed component prematurely.

lessonContentPlans.lessonSummary: Introduce electrified-vehicle architecture through energy flow, voltage-domain separation, safety boundaries, and evidence-based diagnostic reasoning. Learners practice distinguishing observations from conclusions and selecting a documented, vehicle-specific next diagnostic action.

learningObjectives.statement: Describe how an electrified vehicle can store, convert, distribute, and recover electrical energy across propulsion and low-voltage systems.

Distinguish high-voltage and low-voltage system domains, identify their functional relationships, and explain why service boundaries and access controls must be verified from applicable vehicle information.
Interpret fault codes, live data, measurements, operating state, and documented service information as related evidence rather than as isolated proof of a failed component.
Select and justify a safe, vehicle-specific next diagnostic check while documenting what evidence supports the decision and what remains uncertain.

contentBlocks.title: Lesson targets
contentBlocks.description: Establish the system-understanding, safety-boundary, evidence-interpretation, and diagnostic-reasoning outcomes for the lesson.
teachingPoints: Treat the vehicle as an interacting energy and control system rather than a collection of isolated components.
Separate general system concepts from vehicle-specific procedures, values, limits, and access requirements.
Use multiple compatible evidence sources before forming a diagnostic conclusion.
Document uncertainty when the available evidence does not support a final conclusion.
contentBlocks.learnerAction: Classify each lesson target as system understanding, safety reasoning, evidence interpretation, or diagnostic decision-making.

contentBlocks.title: Electrical and diagnostic foundations
contentBlocks.description: Activate prior knowledge of circuits, voltage domains, measurement context, and evidence-based diagnosis.
teachingPoints: Review source, load, conductor, protection, switching, and ground-reference concepts.
Distinguish measured values from commanded or calculated values.
A diagnostic code identifies a detected condition or diagnostic path; it does not by itself prove which component failed.
A measurement has meaning only when its test point, operating state, units, voltage domain, and applicable reference are known.
contentBlocks.learnerAction: Sort sample information into measured, commanded, calculated, observed, documented, or inferred evidence.

contentBlocks.title: Electrified-vehicle energy-flow model
contentBlocks.description: Use a project-authored conceptual model to trace energy among the energy-storage system, power electronics, electric machine, low-voltage system, thermal-management functions, and vehicle loads.
teachingPoints: An energy-storage system supplies electrical energy to the propulsion system according to vehicle operating state and control strategy.
Power-electronic devices can change voltage level or electrical form to support propulsion and auxiliary functions.
An electric machine can consume electrical energy for propulsion and, under applicable operating conditions, return electrical energy during regenerative operation.
Low-voltage systems remain essential for control, communication, wake-up, contactor control, and conventional vehicle loads.
Thermal-management functions influence operating capability and protection across multiple electrified-vehicle systems.
contentBlocks.learnerAction: Trace one propulsion energy path and one regenerative energy path, then mark where the low-voltage system supports control rather than propulsion power.
contentBlocks.sourceBoundary: This is a general instructional model. Actual architecture, component naming, routing, control strategy, and operating limits are vehicle-specific.

contentBlocks.title: Voltage domains and service boundaries
contentBlocks.description: Explain why high-voltage and low-voltage circuits must be identified using documentation, component information, routing, connectors, and verified service information rather than a single visual cue.
teachingPoints: Voltage-domain identification should be based on multiple indicators and applicable service information.
Color, connector appearance, or physical location alone is not sufficient evidence of circuit identity or electrical state.
Isolation, access restrictions, protective equipment, test-equipment suitability, and verification steps depend on the system and the documented service procedure.
A general classroom rule must never replace the approved vehicle-specific disable, isolation, verification, or re-enable procedure.
contentBlocks.learnerAction: Review a generic system map and identify which questions must be answered from vehicle-specific service information before any physical diagnostic access is considered.
contentBlocks.sourceBoundary: No universal high-voltage disable sequence, wait time, test voltage, glove class, measurement category, connector procedure, or acceptance threshold is prescribed by this lesson.

contentBlocks.title: Power conversion and control
contentBlocks.description: Explain the functional roles of DC-DC conversion and inverter control without assuming one universal vehicle topology.
teachingPoints: A DC-DC converter transfers electrical energy between DC voltage domains by changing voltage level as required by the vehicle architecture.
An inverter manages electrical energy between a DC source and an AC electric machine as required by propulsion-system control.
Switching devices are controlled in timed patterns to regulate electrical energy and machine operation.
Some architectures integrate multiple power-electronic functions in one assembly while others distribute them among separate modules.
contentBlocks.learnerAction: Match each functional description to energy conversion, voltage conversion, machine control, or low-voltage support without naming a manufacturer-specific component.
contentBlocks.sourceBoundary: Topology, switching strategy, voltage range, test points, and diagnostic values remain design-specific.

contentBlocks.title: Battery monitoring and thermal context
contentBlocks.description: Connect battery monitoring, state estimation, temperature information, and thermal-management behavior to diagnostic interpretation.
teachingPoints: Battery-management functions can monitor voltage, temperature, current, operating history, and other inputs to support protection and state estimation.
State of charge and state of health are calculated or estimated quantities rather than direct measurements from one voltage reading.
Temperature can affect available power, charging, propulsion behavior, cooling operation, derating, or protective strategies.
A single cell-group difference, temperature value, or state estimate should not be treated as a universal failure threshold without applicable manufacturer criteria.
contentBlocks.learnerAction: Identify which sample battery data items are direct measurements, calculated estimates, operating context, or diagnostic conclusions.
contentBlocks.sourceBoundary: No universal state-of-charge, state-of-health, imbalance, temperature, isolation, or replacement threshold is established.

contentBlocks.title: From concern to evidence-supported next step
contentBlocks.description: Demonstrate how to move from an operating concern to a justified diagnostic next step without prematurely naming a failed component.
teachingPoints: Start with the reported concern and confirm the actual operating condition before interpreting data.
Preserve available fault codes, event information, live data, and operating-state evidence before resets or code clearing.
Correlate low-voltage condition, communication status, propulsion-system state, thermal information, and relevant fault information when they may share a dependency.
Use applicable service information to determine which next test is valid for the identified vehicle and operating state.
Classify the conclusion as supported, not supported, or not yet determined based on the evidence available.
contentBlocks.learnerAction: Given a project-authored scenario with a no-ready concern, low auxiliary voltage, and several communication codes, explain why battery-pack replacement is not justified and identify the additional categories of evidence required before selecting a repair.

providedEvidence: auxiliary-system voltage is below the expected vehicle-specific condition for the current operating state

contentBlocks.sourceBoundary: The scenario is project-authored and contains no universal diagnostic voltage, threshold, or prescribed component replacement decision.

contentBlocks.title: Guided evidence correlation
contentBlocks.description: Practice correlating mixed evidence while maintaining system and safety boundaries.
teachingPoints: Case A: a fault code points to an isolation-monitoring diagnostic path, but the operating state and test history are unknown.
Case B: one battery data value appears unusual, but temperature, load, comparison data, and manufacturer criteria are unavailable.
Case C: a low-voltage supply concern appears at the same time as wake-up and communication faults.
For each case, identify what is known, what is inferred, what remains unknown, and which documentation is needed before a valid next test can be selected.
contentBlocks.learnerAction: Complete a four-column evidence table: known evidence, possible interpretation, missing context, and justified next diagnostic category.

contentBlocks.title: Independent electrified-vehicle diagnostic scenario
contentBlocks.description: Apply the lesson model to a project-authored scenario involving energy flow, voltage-domain reasoning, and mixed diagnostic evidence.
contentBlocks.learnerAction: Produce a short diagnostic plan that traces relevant energy flow, identifies the affected voltage domains, lists evidence to preserve, identifies required service-information checks, and justifies one safe next diagnostic category.
contentBlocks.sourceBoundary: The scenario must remain conceptual until vehicle-specific service information and reviewed technical evidence are supplied.

contentBlocks.title: Architecture and diagnostic reasoning check
contentBlocks.description: Assess whether the learner can distinguish system function, safety boundary, evidence type, and justified next action.
assessmentPrompts: Explain why a diagnostic code does not automatically identify a failed component.

Given mixed evidence, identify which additional evidence would most directly reduce diagnostic uncertainty.

contentBlocks.title: Revise the diagnostic reasoning chain
contentBlocks.description: Use feedback to correct unsupported conclusions, missing context, or unsafe generalizations.
contentBlocks.learnerAction: Revise a diagnostic plan so every conclusion is linked to evidence and every physical test depends on applicable vehicle-specific service information.

contentBlocks.title: Diagnostic evidence record
contentBlocks.description: Document concern, operating state, evidence collected, evidence source, interpretations, uncertainties, selected next action, and verification plan.
contentBlocks.learnerAction: Complete an evidence record that clearly separates observation, documentation, hypothesis, conclusion, and verification.

contentBlocks.title: System, safety, evidence, verification
contentBlocks.description: Summarize the lesson as a repeatable reasoning cycle for electrified-vehicle diagnosis.
teachingPoints: Trace energy flow before isolating a component.
Identify the voltage domain and service boundary before selecting a test.
Correlate multiple evidence sources before naming a cause.
Use vehicle-specific information for procedures, values, access requirements, and acceptance criteria.
Verify the result and document the reasoning chain.

courseModules.title: Battery Systems, Monitoring, and State Estimation
moduleObjectives: Explain how cells, modules, sensing, switching, protection, and control functions interact within an electrified-vehicle energy-storage system.
Differentiate directly measured battery data from calculated or estimated states such as state of charge and state of health.
Interpret battery voltage, current, temperature, isolation-related information, and event history as correlated evidence rather than isolated failure proof.
Develop a vehicle-specific battery diagnostic plan that preserves evidence and avoids unsupported replacement decisions.

lessons.title: Energy-storage architecture
lessons.text: An electrified-vehicle battery system is an interacting electrical, thermal, sensing, switching, protection, and control system. Cells provide electrochemical energy storage; modules and pack structures organize that storage; sensing circuits observe selected operating conditions; switching and protection devices control connection of stored energy to vehicle systems; and control logic uses measured and calculated information to manage operation. The exact arrangement varies by vehicle, so a general architecture model must never be mistaken for a manufacturer-specific wiring diagram or service procedure.
lessons.learnerAction: Create a functional block diagram that separates energy storage, sensing, switching, protection, control, and thermal functions.
lessons.evidenceBoundary: Do not assign universal pack voltage, cell count, module layout, contactor arrangement, fuse rating, or service-disconnect design.

lessons.title: Measured data and calculated states
lessons.text: Battery diagnosis requires separating direct observations from calculated states. Voltage, current, and temperature may be measured through sensors, while state of charge, state of health, available power, remaining energy, and related indicators may be estimated from models that combine several inputs over time. A calculated state can be useful evidence, but it is not equivalent to a direct measurement and should be interpreted with the operating context and applicable service information.
lessons.learnerAction: Classify a mixed battery data set as measured, calculated, commanded, historical, or inferred.
lessons.evidenceBoundary: No universal state-of-charge, state-of-health, imbalance, capacity, temperature, or replacement threshold is established.

lessons.title: Battery evidence correlation
lessons.text: A strong battery diagnosis compares multiple compatible evidence sources. A single unusual voltage, temperature, or estimate may reflect operating state, load, temperature, calibration, sensor behavior, communication quality, or a developing battery condition. Diagnostic reasoning should therefore compare related values, operating conditions, event timing, fault information, and vehicle-specific criteria before identifying a cause.
lessons.learnerAction: Build an evidence table that lists each observation, its possible interpretations, missing context, and the next information needed.
lessons.evidenceBoundary: One data point, one fault code, or one snapshot must not be treated as proof of cell, module, sensor, or pack failure.

practice: Compare direct measurements with calculated battery-state values.
Trace how a sensor concern could affect a calculated battery-state estimate.
Write a battery diagnostic next-step plan that identifies required service information before physical testing.
assessments: Written diagnostic justification with uncertainty statement

courseModules.safetyAndEvidenceBoundary: Battery access, isolation, measurement, PPE, wait times, test equipment, acceptance limits, and replacement criteria are vehicle-specific and require approved authoritative service information.

trainingQuestions.stem: Why should a technician distinguish direct battery measurements from calculated battery-state values?

choices.A: Calculated values are always more accurate than measurements
choices.B: Calculated values may depend on models and multiple inputs, while measurements represent observed sensor or meter data
choices.C: Measurements cannot be used during diagnosis
choices.D: Calculated values never change with operating conditions

trainingQuestions.explanation: Direct measurements and model-derived states are different evidence types. A calculated state should be interpreted with its inputs, operating context, and applicable service information.

trainingQuestions.stem: Which diagnostic approach best supports a battery-system conclusion?

choices.A: Replace the pack after one unusual data point
choices.B: Use the first stored code as proof of failure
choices.C: Correlate voltage, current, temperature, operating state, event history, and applicable service information
choices.D: Ignore calculated values entirely

trainingQuestions.explanation: Battery diagnosis is stronger when compatible evidence is correlated across operating state, measurements, history, and authoritative vehicle information.

trainingQuestions.stem: A reported state-of-charge value should be treated as which type of evidence?

choices.A: A model-derived estimate that should be interpreted with operating context
choices.B: A direct physical measurement of stored energy
choices.C: Proof that the battery is healthy
choices.D: A universal replacement threshold

trainingQuestions.explanation: State of charge is generally an estimated or calculated state, not a direct measurement of stored energy.

trainingQuestions.stem: What is the safest general rule before performing vehicle-specific battery access or isolation work?

choices.A: Use a universal disconnect sequence
choices.B: Follow the applicable vehicle procedure and verify the required electrical state before access
choices.C: Rely on cable color alone
choices.D: Assume the system is safe after the ignition is switched off

trainingQuestions.explanation: Access, isolation, verification, wait times, PPE, and test methods are vehicle-specific and must come from applicable authoritative service information.

courseModules.title: Power Electronics, Electric Machines, and Energy Conversion
moduleObjectives: Explain the functional roles of inverters, DC-DC converters, switching devices, capacitive energy storage, and electric machines.
Trace conceptual energy flow during propulsion, regeneration, and low-voltage support.
Relate commanded operation, measured electrical data, machine state, and thermal information to diagnostic hypotheses.
Select a vehicle-specific diagnostic category without assuming one universal power-electronics topology.

lessons.title: Power conversion functions
lessons.text: Power-electronic assemblies manage electrical energy between voltage domains and between direct-current and alternating-current systems. A traction inverter can control energy transfer between a DC energy source and an electric machine, while a DC-DC converter can support a lower-voltage electrical system from a higher-voltage source. Some vehicles combine these functions; others separate them. Diagnosis begins with identifying the actual architecture before interpreting values or selecting tests.
lessons.learnerAction: Trace conceptual energy paths for propulsion, regeneration, and low-voltage support.
lessons.evidenceBoundary: Do not assume a fixed inverter arrangement, converter direction, nominal voltage, switching frequency, or internal circuit topology.

lessons.title: Electric-machine operation
lessons.text: An electric machine can produce torque when electrical energy is converted to mechanical output and can support regenerative operation when mechanical energy is converted back to electrical energy under permitted conditions. The control system coordinates requested torque, current, speed, position, voltage, and thermal limits. Diagnostic interpretation should compare what was requested, what the system reports, and what the system actually produced.
lessons.learnerAction: Compare commanded torque, machine speed, current, and operating mode in a project-authored scenario.
lessons.evidenceBoundary: Machine type, phase configuration, sensor design, control method, and allowable operating limits are design-specific.

lessons.title: Power-electronics diagnostic evidence
lessons.text: A power-electronics fault may be influenced by electrical supply, control commands, communication, thermal conditions, isolation status, machine behavior, or internal protection. Because several systems interact, a diagnostic code naming an inverter or converter function should be treated as a starting point for a documented diagnostic path rather than an automatic component replacement instruction.
lessons.learnerAction: Develop competing hypotheses for a reduced-propulsion concern and identify evidence that would distinguish among them.
lessons.evidenceBoundary: No single DTC, current value, temperature, or commanded state is sufficient by itself to justify inverter, converter, or electric-machine replacement.

practice: Trace propulsion and regenerative energy conversion.
Compare requested and reported power-electronics states.
Create a hypothesis table for a power-limited operating concern.

visuals.title: DC source, inverter, electric machine, and low-voltage support

courseModules.safetyAndEvidenceBoundary: Opening, probing, discharging, insulation testing, or measuring power-electronic assemblies requires the applicable vehicle procedure, verified electrical state, and suitable equipment.

trainingQuestions.stem: What is the primary diagnostic value of comparing a commanded state with the measured response?

choices.A: It can show whether the system response matches the control request
choices.B: It proves the inverter has failed
choices.C: It eliminates the need for service information
choices.D: It establishes a universal pass/fail current

trainingQuestions.explanation: Comparing request and response helps identify where behavior diverges from control intent without prematurely naming a failed component.

trainingQuestions.stem: Why should a diagnostic code related to an inverter or converter not automatically trigger component replacement?

choices.A: Power-electronics codes are never useful
choices.B: The condition may involve supply, command, communication, thermal, isolation, machine, or internal-protection factors
choices.C: Converters cannot fail
choices.D: Codes only apply to low-voltage systems

trainingQuestions.explanation: Power-electronics operation depends on several interacting systems, so a code is evidence to investigate rather than automatic proof of a failed assembly.

trainingQuestions.stem: During regenerative operation, what general energy relationship is being evaluated?

choices.A: Mechanical energy can be converted to electrical energy under permitted conditions
choices.B: Electrical energy is always converted only to heat
choices.C: The low-voltage battery directly drives the wheels
choices.D: The inverter is bypassed in every vehicle

trainingQuestions.explanation: Regenerative operation can convert vehicle mechanical energy into electrical energy when the vehicle architecture and operating conditions permit it.

trainingQuestions.stem: Before interpreting inverter or DC-DC converter data, what should be established first?

choices.A: The actual vehicle architecture and applicable system information
choices.B: A universal nominal voltage
choices.C: A fixed switching frequency
choices.D: A generic internal circuit diagram

trainingQuestions.explanation: Vehicles differ in topology, integration, voltage domains, and control strategy. Diagnosis begins by identifying the actual architecture.

courseModules.title: Charging Systems, Energy Transfer, and Charge-Readiness Diagnosis
moduleObjectives: Explain the functional difference between external charging equipment, vehicle charge interfaces, onboard conversion functions, and battery charging control.
Trace the information and energy conditions required before charging can begin or continue.
Interpret charge-readiness concerns using vehicle state, external supply information, communication evidence, battery conditions, and thermal context.
Develop a safe diagnostic plan that separates infrastructure, interface, vehicle, and battery-side evidence.

lessons.title: Charging-system boundaries
lessons.text: Charging is a coordinated energy-transfer process involving an external energy source, a connection interface, vehicle control logic, power-conversion functions, battery conditions, and safety interlocks. Depending on the architecture, energy conversion may occur primarily onboard the vehicle or in external equipment. A useful diagnostic model separates the infrastructure side, interface side, vehicle-conversion side, and battery side before drawing conclusions.
lessons.learnerAction: Label the major functional boundaries in a generic charging path.
lessons.evidenceBoundary: Connector standard, pilot signaling, voltage, current, frequency, phase, communication protocol, and charger topology must be verified for the specific vehicle and equipment.

lessons.title: Charge-readiness conditions
lessons.text: A vehicle may evaluate connection status, supply availability, interlock state, battery temperature, battery state, isolation-related information, module communication, scheduled-charge settings, and other conditions before enabling energy transfer. A 'will not charge' complaint therefore does not identify which side of the system is responsible. Diagnosis should first establish whether the vehicle recognizes the connection, whether prerequisites are satisfied, and where the expected sequence stops.
lessons.learnerAction: Construct a readiness sequence from connection detection through energy-transfer authorization.
lessons.evidenceBoundary: No universal enable sequence, timeout, handshake value, or pass/fail voltage is prescribed.

lessons.title: Charging concern isolation
lessons.text: Charging diagnosis becomes more efficient when evidence is grouped by boundary. Infrastructure evidence describes the external source and equipment; interface evidence describes connection and communication; vehicle evidence describes control and conversion; battery evidence describes acceptance conditions; and thermal evidence describes temperature-related limits. Correlating these categories helps avoid replacing vehicle components for an external-supply problem or blaming external equipment for a vehicle-side inhibition.
lessons.learnerAction: Sort a mixed charging complaint into infrastructure, interface, vehicle, battery, and thermal evidence categories.
lessons.evidenceBoundary: Do not infer charger, port, converter, battery, or external-equipment failure from one symptom or one unsuccessful charging attempt.

practice: Map a generic charging energy and information path.
Classify a no-charge concern by system boundary.
Write a test-order rationale that begins with nonintrusive evidence.
courseModules.safetyAndEvidenceBoundary: Charging equipment ratings, connector handling, energized measurements, isolation checks, and internal charger tests require applicable product and vehicle procedures.

trainingQuestions.stem: Which model best helps isolate a no-charge concern?

choices.A: Treat all charging failures as battery failures
choices.B: Separate infrastructure, interface, vehicle, battery, and thermal evidence
choices.C: Replace the charge port first
choices.D: Judge the condition from one unsuccessful charge attempt

trainingQuestions.explanation: Separating the charging system into functional boundaries helps identify where the expected readiness or energy-transfer sequence stops.

trainingQuestions.stem: Why does a 'will not charge' symptom not identify the failed component by itself?

choices.A: Charging involves multiple coordinated prerequisites and system boundaries
choices.B: Charging systems have no diagnostic data
choices.C: External equipment can never affect charging
choices.D: Battery conditions are unrelated to charging

trainingQuestions.explanation: Charging depends on supply, connection, communication, vehicle control, battery acceptance, safety interlocks, and thermal conditions.

trainingQuestions.stem: What is an appropriate first reasoning step when a vehicle will not begin charging?

choices.A: Identify whether the vehicle recognizes the connection and where the expected readiness sequence stops
choices.B: Open the battery pack immediately
choices.C: Assume the external equipment is defective
choices.D: Apply a universal handshake voltage

trainingQuestions.explanation: Establishing connection recognition and readiness state provides nonintrusive evidence before more invasive testing.

courseModules.title: Thermal Management, Protection, and Performance Limiting
moduleObjectives: Explain why temperature management is integrated with battery, power-electronics, electric-machine, cabin, and charging operation.
Differentiate measured temperature, commanded thermal actions, calculated limits, and observed performance changes.
Correlate thermal evidence with operating state before identifying a component fault.
Develop a diagnostic plan for a thermal-related derate or charging limitation.

lessons.title: Thermal-management functions
lessons.text: Electrified vehicles may use liquid, air, refrigerant, or combined thermal strategies to manage batteries, power electronics, electric machines, cabin comfort, and charging performance. Thermal systems can share components or exchange heat across subsystems. Diagnosis therefore requires understanding which thermal path supports the affected function and what operating state existed when the concern occurred.
lessons.learnerAction: Build a system map connecting battery, power electronics, electric machine, cabin, and ambient conditions.
lessons.evidenceBoundary: Coolant routing, refrigerant architecture, pump arrangement, valve strategy, target temperatures, and service procedures are vehicle-specific.

lessons.title: Temperature and protection logic
lessons.text: Temperature information may influence available propulsion power, regenerative capability, charging rate, component protection, and system shutdown decisions. The important diagnostic question is not simply whether a temperature is high or low, but whether the value is plausible, whether the vehicle responded as designed, and whether the applicable limits for that operating state were reached.
lessons.learnerAction: Compare sensor readings, commanded cooling actions, and observed performance in a thermal-limiting scenario.
lessons.evidenceBoundary: No universal temperature threshold, derate point, fan command, pump speed, or charging limit is established.

lessons.title: Thermal diagnostic reasoning
lessons.text: A thermal concern can result from heat generation, inadequate heat transfer, restricted flow, sensor error, actuator performance, control logic, ambient conditions, or another subsystem that changes thermal load. Effective diagnosis compares temperature trends, operating state, command-response relationships, and service information rather than replacing the component named in a protection code.
lessons.learnerAction: Create a cause-and-evidence matrix for a repeated reduced-power event after sustained load.
lessons.evidenceBoundary: Thermal protection codes and temperature readings must be interpreted with vehicle-specific thresholds, sensor locations, and operating conditions.

practice: Map thermal dependencies across vehicle systems.
Differentiate temperature measurement from protection response.
courseModules.safetyAndEvidenceBoundary: Refrigerant, coolant, high-voltage heaters, electric compressors, pumps, and other thermal components require system-specific service precautions and approved procedures.

trainingQuestions.stem: What should be considered when interpreting an unusual component temperature?

choices.A: Only whether the value is numerically high
choices.B: Sensor plausibility, operating state, thermal commands, trends, and applicable vehicle limits
choices.C: The temperature proves the component has failed
choices.D: Thermal data is unrelated to propulsion performance

trainingQuestions.explanation: Temperature becomes useful diagnostic evidence when it is interpreted with operating state, command-response behavior, trends, and vehicle-specific criteria.

trainingQuestions.stem: A reduced-power event that appears with rising temperature should be interpreted how?

choices.A: As automatic proof of battery failure
choices.B: As evidence that may involve thermal protection, heat transfer, sensing, actuator performance, load, or another related condition
choices.C: As proof that the cooling pump is failed
choices.D: Without considering operating conditions

trainingQuestions.explanation: Thermal limiting can have several causes, so trend, command, sensor, and operating evidence should be correlated before reaching a conclusion.

trainingQuestions.stem: Why are universal thermal thresholds inappropriate for AUT-250 training content?

choices.A: Thresholds, sensor locations, cooling strategies, and protection logic vary by vehicle design
choices.B: Temperature never matters
choices.C: All electrified vehicles use identical cooling systems
choices.D: Thermal systems are not serviceable

trainingQuestions.explanation: Vehicle architectures and protection strategies differ, so numeric limits must come from applicable authoritative information.

courseModules.title: Low-Voltage Dependencies, Wake-Up, Communication, and Readiness
moduleObjectives: Explain how low-voltage electrical power supports control modules, communication, contactor control, wake-up, and readiness functions in electrified vehicles.
Recognize how a low-voltage supply concern can create secondary communication and propulsion-system symptoms.
Correlate supply voltage, wake-up state, network communication, module status, and stored faults before escalating to high-voltage diagnosis.
Develop a diagnostic sequence that checks foundational dependencies before component replacement.

lessons.title: Low-voltage system as a control dependency
lessons.text: Although propulsion energy may come from a high-voltage energy-storage system, many control, sensing, communication, and switching functions depend on the low-voltage system. A weak supply, poor connection, unstable ground path, or failed support function can prevent modules from waking, communicating, or commanding high-voltage connection even when the propulsion battery itself is serviceable.
lessons.learnerAction: Trace the control dependency from low-voltage supply to module wake-up, communication, and propulsion readiness.
lessons.evidenceBoundary: Nominal voltage, minimum wake-up voltage, converter support strategy, grounding layout, and readiness criteria must come from applicable vehicle information.

lessons.title: Communication faults as secondary evidence
lessons.text: Multiple communication faults appearing together may indicate a shared power, ground, wake-up, network, or timing dependency. The presence of many codes does not necessarily mean many independent module failures. Diagnostic reasoning should identify which modules were online, which were missing, what common dependencies they share, and whether the fault timing aligns with a supply or wake-up event.
lessons.learnerAction: Group a set of communication codes by possible shared dependency instead of by module name.
lessons.evidenceBoundary: Network topology, termination, biasing, wake-up logic, message timing, and diagnostic criteria are vehicle-specific.

lessons.title: Readiness-first diagnostic strategy
lessons.text: Before escalating to intrusive high-voltage testing, a technician can often gather valuable evidence from low-voltage condition, module communication, readiness indicators, stored event information, and vehicle state. A readiness-first strategy reduces unnecessary access to energized systems and helps identify foundational conditions that can explain several symptoms at once.
lessons.learnerAction: Write a nonintrusive first-pass diagnostic sequence for a vehicle that will not enter propulsion-ready state.
lessons.evidenceBoundary: The sequence defines diagnostic categories, not a universal test order or numeric acceptance criteria.

practice: Trace low-voltage dependencies for propulsion readiness.
Group communication faults by common power, ground, wake-up, or network dependencies.
courseModules.safetyAndEvidenceBoundary: Low-voltage checks do not establish that a high-voltage system is de-energized. High-voltage state must be verified only by the applicable service procedure.

trainingQuestions.stem: Why can a low-voltage supply problem create high-voltage propulsion symptoms?

choices.A: Low-voltage power can support module wake-up, communication, switching control, and readiness functions
choices.B: The low-voltage battery always directly powers the traction motor
choices.C: High-voltage systems do not use control modules
choices.D: Low-voltage faults cannot affect communication

trainingQuestions.explanation: Many control and communication functions required for propulsion readiness depend on stable low-voltage power.

trainingQuestions.stem: Several modules become unavailable at the same time. What should be considered before replacing multiple modules?

choices.A: A shared power, ground, wake-up, network, or timing dependency
choices.B: That all modules failed independently at the same instant
choices.C: Only battery state of charge
choices.D: Only the highest-numbered diagnostic code

trainingQuestions.explanation: Clusters of communication faults may share a foundational dependency, so common causes should be investigated first.

trainingQuestions.stem: What is the purpose of a readiness-first diagnostic strategy?

choices.A: To collect foundational, nonintrusive evidence before escalating to higher-risk testing
choices.B: To skip low-voltage checks
choices.C: To prove the high-voltage system is de-energized
choices.D: To replace control modules more quickly

trainingQuestions.explanation: Low-voltage condition, communication, readiness state, and event history can explain multiple symptoms and can often be evaluated before intrusive testing.

courseModules.title: Advanced Diagnostic Reasoning, Verification, and Documentation
moduleObjectives: Apply a repeatable Request → Measure → Compare → Correlate → Verify diagnostic model to electrified-vehicle concerns.
Develop competing hypotheses and select tests that meaningfully distinguish among them.
Identify when evidence is insufficient to support a repair decision and document uncertainty.
Verify corrective action across the original concern, system state, fault information, and relevant operating conditions.

lessons.title: Request, measure, compare, correlate, verify
lessons.text: Advanced diagnosis is a controlled evidence process. First define what the vehicle or control system is requesting. Then measure or observe the actual response. Compare that response with applicable authoritative information. Correlate the result with other systems and operating conditions. Finally, verify the conclusion with a test or post-repair condition that could reasonably show whether the identified cause was correct.
lessons.learnerAction: Apply the five-stage reasoning model to a mixed propulsion, charging, and thermal complaint.
lessons.evidenceBoundary: The reasoning model is general; every measurement procedure, comparison value, and acceptance criterion remains vehicle-specific.

lessons.title: Competing hypotheses and discriminating tests
lessons.text: A diagnostic plan is stronger when it considers more than one plausible explanation. The technician should ask which evidence would be expected if each hypothesis were true and choose a next check that separates those possibilities efficiently and safely. This prevents confirmation bias and reduces the tendency to replace the first component mentioned by a code or symptom.
lessons.learnerAction: Create three plausible hypotheses and identify one discriminating evidence check for each.
lessons.evidenceBoundary: Hypotheses must remain provisional until supported by compatible evidence and verification.

lessons.title: Verification and documentation
lessons.text: A repair decision is not complete when a part is installed or a code is cleared. Verification should address the original customer concern, relevant system state, fault information, operating conditions, and any related functions affected by the repair. Documentation should preserve the evidence used, the reasoning that connected evidence to the decision, unresolved limitations, and the verification result.
lessons.learnerAction: Complete a diagnostic record containing concern, evidence, hypotheses, decision, repair or action, and verification.
lessons.evidenceBoundary: Clearing codes, observing a single normal reading, or completing one short drive does not automatically establish a successful repair unless it matches the applicable verification criteria.

practice: Apply Request → Measure → Compare → Correlate → Verify to a complex scenario.
Build and rank competing hypotheses by evidentiary support without declaring a cause prematurely.
Design a verification plan that reproduces the relevant operating condition.
courseModules.safetyAndEvidenceBoundary: Diagnostic reasoning does not authorize physical access. Any test involving energized circuits, disabled safety systems, exposed conductors, service disconnects, or high-voltage components requires the applicable approved procedure.

trainingQuestions.stem: In the Request → Measure → Compare → Correlate → Verify model, what does 'Compare' require?

choices.A: Compare the observed response with applicable authoritative information and expected context
choices.B: Compare repair prices
choices.C: Compare only two diagnostic codes
choices.D: Assume the requested state is correct

trainingQuestions.explanation: The comparison step evaluates observed behavior against applicable criteria or expected system behavior before correlation and verification.

trainingQuestions.stem: Why should a technician develop competing hypotheses during a complex diagnosis?

choices.A: To choose evidence checks that distinguish among plausible explanations and reduce confirmation bias
choices.B: To avoid collecting evidence
choices.C: To make every possible repair
choices.D: To select the first component mentioned by a code

trainingQuestions.explanation: Competing hypotheses encourage discriminating tests and make it less likely that one early clue will dominate the diagnosis.

trainingQuestions.stem: What makes post-repair verification stronger than simply clearing codes?

choices.A: It checks whether the original concern and relevant system behavior are actually resolved under appropriate conditions
choices.B: It guarantees no future faults
choices.C: It removes the need for documentation
choices.D: It proves every related component is new

trainingQuestions.explanation: Verification should address the original concern, relevant operating state, fault information, and system response rather than relying on code clearing alone.
